profile.behavior: Agile canopy forager that gleans insects, fruit, and nectar from foliage, sometimes hangs upside down or sallies from a perch for flying insects; the female weaves a suspended, pouch-shaped nest from slender fibers.
field_marks: Solid-black head and upper back in adult males
Black wings with a bold white wing bar and orange shoulder patch
Long black tail with orange outer feathers
profile.habitat: Open deciduous woodland, forest edges, riverside trees, small groves, orchards, parks, and gardens; outside the breeding season also uses open woodland, flowering trees, and shade-grown plantations.

findings: The primary specimen is an anatomically coherent adult male Baltimore Oriole with one head and bill, two legs gripping the branch, a normal single tail, and two anatomically implied wings with the far wing naturally obscured by the lateral pose.

Plumage agrees with the field references and direct sources: solid-black head and upper back, brilliant orange breast, belly, and rump, black wings, a broad white wing bar, orange shoulder coverts, and orange outer tail feathers surrounding a black tail center.

The long, thick-based, sharply pointed bill is consistent across the primary specimen and detached head study. Both mandibles trace cleanly from a shared base to a sharp, essentially co-terminal tip, matching the clearest closed-bill reference profiles; neither bill is truncated, reversed, or malformed.

The dark eyes, gray legs, feet, body proportions, wing structure, and tail arrangement are coherent and species-appropriate. The detached wing and head are clearly isolated supplementary studies and do not appear attached to the primary specimen.

The common name, scientific name, and family are correctly printed as “Baltimore Oriole,” “Icterus galbula,” and “Icteridae.” Smithsonian and Animal Diversity Web independently confirm Icterus galbula in Icteridae.

The printed measurements—length 17–19 cm (6.7–7.5 in), wingspan 23–30 cm (9.1–11.8 in), and weight 30–40 g (1.1–1.4 oz)—exactly match Cornell’s published measurements. The repeated BODY LENGTH value also agrees.

The habitat and behavior paragraphs reproduce the proposed wording completely and coherently, with no duplicated, omitted, substituted, misspelled, or nonsensical words. Their substance is supported by the direct Cornell life-history page.
All six field-mark lines and all five palette labels are present and correctly worded. The palette accurately reflects the illustrated adult-male colors.

The vertical length ruler is explicitly labeled “SCHEMATIC — NOT TO SCALE,” increases from 17 cm at the bottom to 19 cm at the top, has matching imperial endpoints, and contains exactly four evenly spaced unlabeled interior ticks forming five proportional segments. No separate measurement marker disagrees with it.
The plate contains no observation locality, ZIP code, coordinates, map, or other local-observation detail; “Baltimore” appears only as part of the required common name.
